claims.text: Controlled coherent nanoprecipitation can enhance the high-temperature mechanical strength of refractory high-entropy alloys.
Controlled coherent nanoprecipitation can enhance the thermoelastic stability of refractory high-entropy alloys.
Small additions of Hf and Mo can promote coherent nanoprecipitate formation in refractory high-entropy alloys.
Tailored thermomechanical processing can be used to induce controlled coherent nanoprecipitates.
The intended structural mediator is a uniform distribution of coherent nanoprecipitates in the matrix.
Coherent nanoprecipitates act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Coherent nanoprecipitates modify local lattice-diffusion paths.
The nanoprecipitates reduce dislocation climb at elevated temperatures.
The nanoprecipitates slow diffusional creep at elevated temperatures.
Relative to a homogeneous solid-solution baseline, the nanoprecipitate-containing alloy will have higher elevated-temperature yield strength.
Relative to the baseline, the nanoprecipitate-containing alloy will have a lower elevated-temperature creep rate.
Relative to the baseline, the nanoprecipitate-containing alloy will retain a more stable thermoelastic modulus at elevated temperatures.
The proposed comparison applies under tensile and creep loading from approximately 600 to 900 degrees Celsius.
The beneficial effects should remain observable at service temperatures up to 900 degrees Celsius.
The predicted benefits may fail outside the stated temperature range or when the nanoprecipitate phases are unstable.
The quantitative effects of nanoprecipitate size, volume fraction, and distribution on dislocation mobility and diffusion rates are not yet determined.
A controlled test will compare a nanoprecipitate-treated refractory HEA with a homogeneous-microstructure baseline under identical tensile and creep conditions.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in yield strength, creep rate, and thermoelastic-modulus stability is specified as a falsifying outcome.
